verses.text: Ahithophel also told Absalom, “Let me pick twelve thousand men and go after David tonight.
I'll catch him worn out and exhausted and frighten him. Everyone with him will run away. I'll strike down the king alone
and bring everyone else back to you. Once you've dealt with the one man you're after, it's as good as having everyone back. All the people will be at peace.”
Absalom and all Israel's elders liked the plan.
Then Absalom said, “Call Hushai the Archite too. Let's hear what he has to say.”
When Hushai came in, Absalom told him what Ahithophel had said and asked, “Should we do what he says? If you disagree, speak up.”
Hushai answered, “This time Ahithophel's advice is no good.”

He went on, “You know your father and his men. They're tough fighters and as fierce as a bear in the wild that's lost her cubs. Your father knows war. He won't spend the night with the rest of the people.
He's already hiding in a pit or somewhere else. If some of your men fall in the first attack, anyone who hears of it will say, ‘Absalom's followers are being slaughtered!’
Even the bravest man, with a heart like a lion's, will lose his nerve. All Israel knows your father is a mighty warrior and the men with him are brave fighters.
Here's my advice. Gather all Israel to you, from Dan to Beersheba, as many as the grains of sand by the sea, and lead them into battle yourself.
We'll catch up with him wherever he is and fall on him the way dew settles on the ground. Neither he nor any of his men will survive.
If he retreats into a city, all Israel will bring ropes and drag the city into the river until there's not even a pebble left.”
Absalom and all the Israelite men said, “Hushai the Archite's advice is better than Ahithophel's.” The LORD had decided to overturn Ahithophel's sound advice and bring disaster on Absalom.
Then Hushai told Zadok and Abiathar the priests, “Here's what Ahithophel told Absalom and the elders of Israel, and here's what I advised.
Send word to David right away: ‘Don't spend the night at the wilderness crossings. Get across, or the king and everyone with him could be wiped out.’”
Jonathan and Ahimaaz were staying near En Rogel. A servant woman would pass messages to them, and they would take the messages to King David. They couldn't risk being seen entering the city.
A boy spotted them and told Absalom. Both men hurried away to a house in Bahurim. The owner had a well in his courtyard, and the two went down into it.
The woman of the house covered the mouth of the well and spread crushed grain on top. Nobody noticed a thing.

Absalom's servants came to the house and asked her, “Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?” She told them, “They've crossed the stream.” The men searched, found no trace of them, and went back to Jerusalem.

After the men left, Ahimaaz and Jonathan climbed out of the well and went to King David. “Get up and cross the water quickly,” they told him. Then they explained what Ahithophel had advised against him.
David got up, and he and everyone with him crossed the Jordan. By daybreak, every last one of them had made it across.
When Ahithophel saw that his advice hadn't been followed, he saddled his donkey and went home to his town. He put his affairs in order and hanged himself. He died and was buried in his father's tomb.
David reached Mahanaim. Absalom crossed the Jordan with all his Israelite troops.
Absalom put Amasa in command of the army in Joab's place. Amasa was the son of Ithra the Israelite and Abigail daughter of Nahash. Abigail was the sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother.
Absalom and Israel camped in the land of Gilead.
When David arrived in Mahanaim, Shobi son of Nahash from the Ammonite city of Rabbah, Machir son of Ammiel from Lo Debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim
brought beds, basins, clay pots, wheat, barley, flour, parched grain, beans, lentils, roasted grain,
honey, butter, sheep, and cheese from the herd for David and his people to eat. “These people have grown hungry, tired, and thirsty in the wilderness,” they said.
